title: East Hampton: An Agreement, Reserved Rights and Settler Control
summary: Four Native leaders and two English colonial governors are named in East Hampton’s 1648 agreement. Its retained fishing, hunting and wampum-shell rights show why a deed cannot be read as the end of Native relationships with land and water.
address_label: Wainscott to Napeague regional history — not a visitor entrance
map_geometry_source: Approximate mainland regional interpretation, not a deed survey; original 1648 bounds, Rountree/Strong historical diagram, modern town and coastline orientation.
why_this_matters: The paper that supported an English town also recorded Native rights that continued within it. Reading the named parties, retained activities and later transfer to settlers together shows how land claims could grow without Native people or their relationships disappearing.
introduction_title: Land, agreements and continuing Native rights
introduction_content: Four Native leaders and two English colonial governors are named in East Hampton’s 1648 agreement. Its retained fishing, hunting and wampum-shell rights show why a deed cannot be read as the end of Native relationships with land and water.
history_title: Who made the agreement, and what followed?
history_content:
A place before it became an English town

This landscape lies on Long Island's South Fork, from the Southampton side of present-day Wainscott toward Napeague, west of Montauk's higher ground. Long before an English town was organized here, Native communities governed and used its fields, woods, ponds and shore. The 1648 agreement itself records that presence: it names four Native leaders and protects activities that connected their communities to these places. It is evidence of negotiations within an inhabited Native homeland, not the discovery of vacant land. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

The area shown here concerns the first East Hampton agreement. Gardiners Island and the later agreements involving Hither Woods and eastern Montauk have separate histories. Combining them into one sale would conceal the successive steps by which settlers extended their claims. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I [2] Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montauketts of Eastern Long Island

Who made the agreement?

On April 29, 1648, the written agreement named Theophilus Eaton, governor of the English colony of New Haven, and Edward Hopkins, governor of the English colony of Connecticut, with their associates. On the Native side it named Poggatacut of Munhansett, Wayandanch of Meuntacut, Momowetow of Corchake and Nowedonah of Shinecoke. These historical spellings refer to leaders associated with Manhansett, Montaukett, Corchaug and Shinnecock communities. The signature list records Chectanoo as interpreter. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

The involvement of several leaders matters. This was not an unnamed settler receiving land from an undifferentiated group of “Indians.” Nor does the presence of several sachems prove that any one of them governed every Native community on Long Island. The document records particular parties to an agreement; it cannot supply every community member's understanding or consent. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

What land did the paper describe?

The agreement described land between Southampton inhabitants' bounds and the east side of Napeak, beside the Montauk highland, across the width of the island from sea to sea. It expressly avoided encroaching on land Southampton could establish it lawfully possessed. The consideration recorded was twenty coats, twenty-four each of looking glasses, hoes, hatchets and knives, and one hundred items transcribed as “muges.” The last term is left in its historical form here rather than guessed from the transcription. These were the stated terms, not a basis for calculating a modern fair price or assuming equal bargaining power. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

The wording describes an enduring transfer to the purchasers and their heirs. But reading that wording alone gives an incomplete account: the agreement also records continuing Native rights within the same landscape. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

Fishing, hunting and wampum remained part of the agreement

The Native parties reserved fishing in creeks and ponds and hunting in the woods, with a condition concerning injury to English inhabitants' goods and livestock. They retained access to shells for making wampum and to the fins and tails of stranded whales. Another clause divided a deer between an English person who killed it in the water and the Native sachem when Native hunters had driven it there. These provisions concerned food, materials and continuing relations with the shore and woods. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

Rights to use a place or its resources are sometimes described as use-rights, or usufruct rights. Here they are not merely a modern theory applied to the past: particular retained activities are written into the agreement. The deed's transfer language and these reservations have to be read together. The record does not prove that the protections were consistently honored afterward, or that the Native parties intended to surrender every form of authority over their homeland. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

From negotiations to control by a settler town

On April 16, 1651, Edward Hopkins recorded that East Hampton's inhabitants had reimbursed him and that he delivered the purchase papers and the interest acquired through them to the inhabitants. This was a further step in the claim's history: papers made in the governors' names became the basis for the English settlement's possession and administration. It was not a second Native agreement. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

The distinction helps explain how dispossession worked through more than a signature. A colonial document could preserve Native access while also supporting a settler institution that assigned land and managed its use. Subsequent transactions farther east extended English claims toward Montauk. Their dates and conditions belong in their own accounts; the 1648 agreement should not be made to stand for all of them. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I [2] Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montauketts of Eastern Long Island

Town orders narrowed the space for Native life

A year earlier, on May 28, 1655, the town had ordered "for the prevention of abuse amongst the Indians by selling of strong water" that no one carry liquor to Native people or sell it to them in town, except to those "sent by the Sachem" with "a writine ticket from him," a ticket the town gave him, and never more than a quart at a time. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

On November 24, 1656, East Hampton's town record prohibited letting land to Native people for planting, with a penalty of two pounds per acre. It required the town's permission before Native people could establish wigwams within its bounds, and imposed a two-pound-ten-shilling penalty for Native trapping. The order also restricted Native travel and carrying burdens through town on the Sabbath, backed by corporal punishment. These were acts of an English settler government claiming authority over Native cultivation, homes, food gathering and movement. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

This is a concrete part of the land-loss story. Eight years after an agreement that retained hunting and other uses, the town sought to make important activities dependent on its permission or punishable under its rules. The order does not show how every clause was enforced or identify every affected household. It does show that losing land involved restrictions on living and using it, as well as transfers recorded on paper. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

Smallpox, 1663

On March 2, 1662/63, during an outbreak of smallpox, the town ordered "that noe Indian shall come to towne in to the street" after notice, on penalty of five shillings or a whipping, "untill they be free of the small poxe." They could still come to the back side of houses and call. Any English person or Native servant who went to the wigwams would suffer the same punishment. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

Storage pits at Montauk, 1668

Twelve years later, the town and the Montaukett reached another agreement about life on the land. On December 21, 1668, before the commissioners John Howell and John Youngs, East Hampton's inhabitants and "the Indians of Montaukut" agreed that every man would secure his "barne" at Montauk from English cattle and horses. If a Native owner neglected his and an animal died, they would all make good the damage, and old barns with no particular owner were to be pointed out so they could be filled up. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

These barns were not buildings. A draft recorded two days earlier, crossed out in the town book, speaks of English animals that "fall in" and of filling up the old ones: they were pits dug in the ground to store food. The agreement shows English livestock grazing on Montaukett land, and the Montaukett made answerable for the animals around their own food stores. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I

Dogs, a lease and the town's claims, 1683

On January 23, 1682/83, a town meeting voted that the Native people be warned to kill all their dogs except one to a wigwam; if they did not within a fortnight, it would be "Lawfull for any English to kill all ye Indians doggs yt they can meete withall." Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume II, printed p. 118

Eight days later the town voted to contest a lease. "Nat Indian" had leased land at Montauk to Josiah Hobart, land the town said had been given to it. Thomas Baker and Thomas Talmage were to gather the Native people "to see if they will Maintaine our right in ye land" and prepare for a trial. A Montaukett man was acting as an owner of Montauk land, and the town needed Montaukett testimony to defend its own claim. Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume II, printed p. 118

Montauk, 1701

On June 30, 1701, a town committee rode to Montauk to treat with the Montaukett about a difference the town later traced to yearly payments the Montaukett said were owed them. Several Montaukett met the committee "but would not own there was any difference between them and us, but did generally forbid that the sheep should be beyond the ditch." The committee offered to make good any damage the sheep did to Montaukett cornfields. Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume III, printed pp. 7 and 29–30

Native people did not disappear when the town's claims grew

The longer Montaukett story includes work, family networks and continued residence under increasingly restrictive conditions. Allison Manfra McGovern's study of Montaukett labor and survivance examines those experiences through documentary and archaeological evidence. Land transactions are one part of that history, not a record of a people ending. [2] Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montauketts of Eastern Long Island

Continue to the Montauk auction landscape, Indian Fields and Freetown accounts to follow later struggles over land and removal. Those later events should not be projected backward as if they happened everywhere in 1648. Likewise, contemporary LandBack and restoration should be understood through the priorities of living Native communities, rather than an assumption that this historical deed settles today's questions of authority, access or justice. [2] Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montauketts of Eastern Long Island

Continue with the existing 1648 leadership account in Montaukett Ancestral Land, and the later histories of the Montauk auction, Indian Fields and Freetown.
whereintheworld_content: The shaded area on the map shows the approximate region, not a seventeenth-century survey. The deed supplies the broad relationship between Southampton and Napeague; the historical diagram separates this tract from later Montauk transactions. Modern shorelines and the present town boundary help orient the reader, but they are not proof of unchanged 1648 boundaries. Detached islands are excluded. The eastern line through the lowland-to-highland transition is interpretive. It locates the transition from the Napeague lowland to the Montauk highland rather than a measured historic boundary. No signing place, private home or archaeological location is identified. [1] Records of the Town of East Hampton, volume I [2] Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montauketts of Eastern Long Island [3] Hither Hills State Park map
